overview.title: Perception, explained.
overview.metaTitle: Learn about perception and browser experiments | Sense6
overview.description: Five guides to colour vision, reaction time, hearing and visual sharpness, with research sources and practical explanations of browser-test limits.
overview.intro: A colour gradient, a reaction time in milliseconds, a tone you can barely hear: each seems to offer a simple answer about your senses. These five guides explain what is being tested, how the equipment affects the result, and where the research fits. Each links to a Sense6 experiment you can try.
overview.boundary: Sense6 is a recreational browser lab. Its experiments are not clinically validated and cannot diagnose a condition or establish a biological trait.

tetrachromacy-guide.title: Can an online test detect tetrachromacy?
tetrachromacy-guide.metaTitle: Can an online test detect tetrachromacy? | Sense6
tetrachromacy-guide.description: What an extra cone signal would mean, why counting bands in a gradient cannot establish it, and what the Screen Colour Lab actually records.
tetrachromacy-guide.summary: No ordinary RGB-screen test can demonstrate functional tetrachromacy. Distinguishing small colour differences on a screen is a different task from showing that someone uses a fourth independent signal for colour vision.

sections.heading: An extra photopigment is only part of the story
paragraphs: Most human colour vision starts with three classes of cone photoreceptors, with overlapping sensitivities to light. Functional tetrachromacy would add an independent dimension of colour discrimination. It does not simply mean noticing more shades or knowing more colour names.

Some inherited variations can produce an additional class of cone photopigment, particularly in carriers of certain X-linked colour-vision variants. For that extra signal to matter perceptually, the visual system must use it to distinguish colours that would otherwise match. The presence of four photopigments alone does not settle the question.

Jordan and colleagues combined colour-matching and discrimination tasks with genetic analysis in their 2010 study. Their evidence depended on purpose-built stimuli and comparisons between observers. It was a study of functional colour vision, not a recipe for identifying tetrachromats from a colourful image.

sections.heading: A gradient still comes from three display primaries
paragraphs: An ordinary RGB display mixes light from red, green and blue components. Changing their intensities produces many colours, but more shades do not add another independent primary. A wide-gamut display can extend the available colours without turning a three-primary image into a fourth-cone test.

Counting bands in a gradient tells you what boundaries you noticed in that image. It cannot show whether a fourth cone signal contributed. Even a demanding colour task needs stimuli designed to separate three-cone matches from possible four-cone discrimination before it can address tetrachromacy.

The CSS Color specification explains how browsers describe and convert colours. That is an engineering reference for the displayed values; it does not measure the light from your screen. Brightness settings, colour filters and room lighting remain part of the viewing conditions.

sections.heading: Three tasks in the Screen Colour Lab
paragraphs: Sense6 asks you to pick a different tile, choose a different dot field, and arrange a sequence of hues. These tasks put different demands on your attention. Finding an odd tile is a local comparison; ordering a row requires comparing several colours with one another.

In the tile and dot-field tasks, correct responses make the difference smaller and errors make it larger. The result shows where each short adaptive sequence ended, alongside response counts and the range presented. An ending level is not a stable threshold: a few late choices can still move it.

Hue ordering has its own result. Sense6 keeps it separate from the two adaptive levels rather than averaging unlike tasks into a colour-vision score. All three describe your choices among colours rendered by this browser on this display.

sections.heading: Reading a repeat
paragraphs: Keep the display, brightness and lighting similar if you repeat the lab. Note a filter change or a different screen before interpreting a change in the result. The private journal keeps attempts separate; it does not pool them or retain only a best run.

A repeat can help you inspect how your choices varied under similar conditions. It cannot answer the laboratory question about an extra perceptual dimension. For that, the relevant evidence is controlled colour discrimination with suitable spectral stimuli and comparison observers.

experiment.hint: Three separate screen-relative observations · about 4 minutes · no tetrachromacy diagnosis

reaction-time-guide.title: How accurate is a reaction-time test in a browser?
reaction-time-guide.metaTitle: How accurate are browser reaction-time tests? | Sense6
reaction-time-guide.description: Where display and input delays enter a browser reaction time, how to read a median, and which conditions to keep steady when repeating Riflessi.
reaction-time-guide.summary: A browser reaction time includes delays from the display and input device as well as your response. It is not an instrument-calibrated measurement of human reflex speed. Using the same setup makes repeats easier to interpret, but does not remove those delays.

sections.heading: From a colour change to a key press
paragraphs: Imagine a circle changing colour and you pressing a key when you see it. The page first schedules the change. The display then shows it, you respond, and the keyboard and operating system deliver an event to the browser. The recorded interval spans parts of this chain that the page cannot measure separately.

Display lag occurs before the visible signal reaches you. Keyboard lag occurs after you press the key, before the response reaches the software. A precise browser clock cannot identify either physical moment on its own. That would require external equipment, such as a light sensor and a way to measure the physical response.

Switching from a key to a touchscreen also changes how you respond, as well as the input hardware. If the recorded time changes, the result alone cannot say how much came from your movement and how much from the device. The illustration on this page separates assumed delays to explain this distinction; it does not measure yours.

sections.heading: Accuracy and consistency are different
paragraphs: A setup can add a fairly consistent delay and still give closely grouped readings. Those readings may be precise without being accurate to the physical interval. Variable delays create another problem: they add scatter, which can obscure small differences between runs.

Bridges and colleagues tested laboratory and online experiment tools using external timing equipment. Anwyl-Irvine and colleagues examined browser and device combinations, including responses made with consumer keyboards. Their findings concern the tested software and equipment. They establish neither a universal browser offset nor a correction you can apply to Sense6.

sections.heading: Read the run, not just the fastest response
paragraphs: Riflessi reports the median of valid responses and their spread. The median is the middle recorded value, so one unusually slow response has less influence than it would on a mean. It still needs context: a tidy median can come from a run with missed signals or many excluded responses.

Check the scheduled and valid event counts, false starts and interruption notes. Pressing before the signal is anticipation, not a faster successful response. Losing focus or switching tabs can disrupt an attempt; the experiment pauses and discards the interrupted event rather than treating it as an ordinary response.

The short Segnale scope asks for a response to one signal. Scelta adds a left-or-right choice. The complete scope also includes a sustained-response block. A choice time includes deciding which response to make, so it should not be compared with a simple-response time as though both measured the same task.

sections.heading: Repeating Riflessi on one setup
paragraphs: Use the same device and chosen input method, keep the tab visible, and complete the practice before the measured run. If you switch keyboards or screens, record that change. Similar conditions reduce ambiguity; they do not guarantee that every difference reflects practice or attention.

The local journal records the scope and setup alongside the results. Compare compatible runs and look at the spread and event counts as well as the median. A limited or interrupted run may tell you more about that attempt than about a change in your response speed.
The link here opens Segnale with its normal setup and consent step. Your response times stay in this browser. Sense6 has no global leaderboard or clinical interpretation of the result.

color-blindness-guide.title: What can an online colour-blindness test tell you?
color-blindness-guide.metaTitle: What can an online colour-blindness test tell you? | Sense6
color-blindness-guide.description: Why dot plates and noisy gap tasks differ, how brightness can become a clue, and how to interpret Daltonia’s separate display-colour tracks.
color-blindness-guide.summary: An online task can record which displayed colour differences you distinguished. It cannot, by itself, confirm or rule out a colour-vision deficiency. The screen and the task design both affect what the result means.

sections.heading: Colour blindness does not usually mean no colour
paragraphs: Colour-vision deficiency affects the ability to distinguish particular colour differences. Most people described as colour blind still see many colours. The difficulty is selective, rather than a general inability to see colour.

Professional assessment can use dot plates with embedded shapes, hue-arrangement tasks or an anomaloscope, which asks the observer to match lights. These tasks make different comparisons. The National Eye Institute explains their uses; one online result cannot supply the clinical interpretation of an appropriately administered assessment.

sections.heading: Brightness can give the answer away
paragraphs: A coloured shape may stand out because it is brighter than its background, even when the intended colour difference is difficult to see. A task meant to study colour discrimination needs to account for that alternative clue.

Printed dot plates depend on their colours and viewing conditions. A photograph or screenshot introduces another set of changes before the image reaches your display. Screen brightness, night-light filters and room lighting can further alter what you see. Recognising a number in that image is not equivalent to completing the original test under its specified conditions.

Regan, Reffin and Mollon’s laboratory method used varying dot luminance and masking contours to make brightness and shape clues less useful. The method provides background for noisy-dot discrimination tasks. It does not establish that every browser adaptation isolates colour in the same way.

sections.heading: Daltonia asks you to find a gap
paragraphs: In Sense6’s Daltonia task, a C-shaped target sits among noisy dots. You choose the direction of its gap, or indicate that no gap is visible. The run samples three display-colour directions independently, making each track harder or easier in response to your choices.

The dot noise is intended to reduce brightness clues, but it does not guarantee that the target is distinguishable only by colour. Residual luminance differences can remain. Daltonia is a custom display task, not an Ishihara plate or a certified reproduction of the Cambridge Colour Test.

High-contrast control presentations check whether you can perform the gap response when the target is easier to see. Missing one can reflect difficulty with the task or an unreliable attempt. Getting them right supports the interpretation of that run; it does not classify your colour vision.

sections.heading: What the three ending levels mean
paragraphs: Each adaptive result belongs to a direction in the software’s display-colour model. A level is not a cone-sensitivity measurement or a universal ranking of your eyes. The three values should remain separate: averaging them would hide which displayed comparisons were difficult.

Read the control responses and track evidence alongside the levels. A reversal is a change in the direction of the adaptive sequence as responses switch between success and error. A short track with few reversals offers limited evidence about where performance settles. Reaching the easiest or hardest allowed level also leaves a bound, rather than an exact threshold.

For a repeat, keep the screen, filters and room lighting similar, and use a similar viewing position. The private journal stores runs with their setup and method so incompatible attempts can be identified. If colour distinctions are causing difficulty in daily life or affect an occupational requirement, take that concern to an eye-care professional; Daltonia cannot resolve it.

hearing-range-guide.title: Can a browser test your hearing range?
hearing-range-guide.metaTitle: Can a browser test your hearing range? | Sense6
hearing-range-guide.description: Why a tone’s frequency does not tell you its level at your ears, what Udito’s setup checks establish, and how its results differ from audiometry.
hearing-range-guide.summary: A browser can generate tones, but it cannot know their sound pressure at your ears. The highest frequency noticed on one setup is not an audiogram, a diagnosis of hearing loss, or a measure of hearing age.

sections.heading: Frequency tells only part of the story
paragraphs: Frequency, measured in hertz (Hz), describes how rapidly a sound vibrates. Whether you can hear a tone also depends on its level. A browser can set a digital frequency and amplitude, but the actual headphone output depends on everything between that signal and your ears.

The same position on a volume slider does not mean the same sound pressure with two different headphones. Changing their fit can change what reaches you too. If a tone disappears after a headphone swap, that alone cannot establish a change in hearing.

Clinical pure-tone audiometry measures sensitivity to calibrated sounds at selected frequencies, commonly reported in decibels hearing level (dB HL). The American Speech-Language-Hearing Association specifies equipment calibration, transducer and test-environment requirements. A browser tone with an unknown acoustic level cannot provide that measurement.

sections.heading: The browser does not measure your headphones
paragraphs: The Web Audio specification describes digital sound generation and processing. The audio context reports a sample rate, which places a mathematical limit on frequency generation. It does not report the acoustic response of your headphones. A tone that exists in the software may be poorly reproduced by the playback equipment.

Headphone response varies with frequency. Background noise can mask a quiet tone, while audio processing or a different earbud seal can change audibility. These effects matter when interpreting a high-frequency result; the browser has no calibrated microphone at your ear to separate them.

Choose a comfortable volume and stop if a sound is uncomfortable. Do not turn the volume up to chase a higher frequency. Keeping volume unchanged makes choices within a run easier to compare, but it neither calibrates the output nor guarantees a safe sound level on every device.

sections.heading: What Udito checks before reporting a result
paragraphs: Udito starts with presentation checks intended to give evidence of headphone-like listening. Passing them does not identify the physical device or measure its output. The setup also asks you to confirm audibility of reference tones before proceeding.

The Focused scope then follows an adaptive frequency sequence and reports its upper run boundary. Standard adds separate pitch-difference tasks near selected reference frequencies. Finding a small pitch difference and hearing a high-frequency tone are different tasks, so their results are not combined into a hearing score.

Control responses, interruptions and your final confirmation about unchanged volume accompany the result. Read any caution reasons before comparing attempts. If the frequency sequence reaches the software’s ceiling, the result says that the task stopped there. It does not locate the highest frequency you could hear.

Repeat with the same headphones, connection and comfortable volume setting if you want to compare sessions. The private journal keeps the task and setup with each entry. A change of equipment can make two otherwise similar runs unsuitable for comparison.

sections.heading: A hearing check uses its own method
paragraphs: WHO’s hearWHO app asks users to identify spoken digits in background noise. Evidence for that hearing check belongs to its digits-in-noise method; it does not validate Udito’s tone tasks. WHO also states that hearWHO does not replace consulting a health professional.

Trouble following conversations or a change in hearing deserves an appropriate professional assessment. A recreational frequency result cannot determine whether you need hearing aids. Use Udito to inspect your listening choices on a known setup, rather than as a record of clinical hearing thresholds.

visual-acuity-guide.title: Can an online visual-acuity test replace an eye exam?
visual-acuity-guide.metaTitle: Can an online visual-acuity test replace an eye exam? | Sense6
visual-acuity-guide.description: How pixel size and viewing distance affect a small target, what Acutezza’s model interval covers, and why sharpness is only part of an eye examination.
visual-acuity-guide.summary: No. A screen task can record which small shapes you identified at a stated distance. It cannot establish eye health, prescribe lenses, or replace an eye examination. Its estimate also depends on how accurately the display scale and viewing distance were set.

sections.heading: Pixels need a physical size and a viewing distance
paragraphs: Move closer to a small ring on a screen and its gap occupies a larger angle at your eye. The pixel count has not changed, but the viewing task has. A sharpness estimate therefore needs both the target’s physical size and your distance from it.

A CSS pixel is a browser layout unit, not necessarily one physical dot on the panel. Page zoom and operating-system scaling affect the rendered size. A ring with the same CSS dimensions can occupy a different physical space on another screen; matching pixel counts alone does not make the viewing conditions equivalent.

ISO 8596 describes Landolt-ring presentation for distance-vision certification or licensing. Its stated scope excludes clinical measurement. It supplies context for the ring design, not certification of Sense6’s self-administered task.

sections.heading: Identifying a gap is a specific task
paragraphs: A Landolt ring is a broken circle whose gap can face different directions. Choosing the direction asks you to resolve that detail at the displayed size and contrast. The task is narrower than assessing your sight in everyday conditions, and does not yield a lens prescription.

Acutezza uses a short response sequence to estimate angular detail. The reported model interval describes uncertainty within the scoring model. It does not include every possible error in card matching, viewing distance or screen output. A narrow interval can accompany a setup that was only approximately measured.

The display also limits how small a gap can be rendered. At a software floor or ceiling, the result is bounded by the available targets. Read the boundary flag before treating the displayed estimate as an exact limit of what you can resolve.

sections.heading: Keep eye and contrast conditions separate
paragraphs: Acutezza asks you to check the on-screen scale against a physical card and establish a viewing distance. The setup’s provenance matters: a measured distance and an assumed one are not equally informative. Moving during the task can also change the visual angle after setup is complete.

The Focused scope uses a high-contrast target. Standard adds a nominal low-contrast condition when the setup permits it. “Nominal” refers to the intended rendered contrast: Sense6 does not measure the screen’s light output. An estimate from the fainter condition needs its own interpretation.

Results stay separate for each eye and condition. The session records scale and distance information, control responses, display changes and bounds. Those details explain what went into the estimate. They are especially useful if one condition was incomplete or a setup check required caution.

For repeats, keep your correction and room lighting consistent, use the same display, and recheck the distance. Compare compatible conditions in the local journal. Acutezza does not convert the estimates into a 20/20 claim, an astigmatism axis, driving eligibility or an overall vision grade.

sections.heading: An eye examination looks beyond sharpness
paragraphs: The National Eye Institute describes a dilated eye examination that includes acuity, visual fields, eye-muscle function, pupil response and eye pressure, as well as inspection inside the eye. Resolving a small on-screen gap cannot check the retina or optic nerve.

If your vision changes or you have symptoms, seek an eye-care professional’s assessment. Sudden vision loss, severe pain, new flashes or floaters, or a curtain over your field of view warrant prompt professional attention. A good result in a browser task should never be used to delay care.
